nodes.name: Pure Cu2O synthesis
nodes.procedure: Solution A was prepared by dissolving 2g of copper acetate in 25 mL of distilled water, and stirring at 70°C for 10 min to completely dissolve it. In another separate vessel, 1.6g NaOH and 1.4g ascorbic acid was dissolved in 20 mL distilled water to prepare solution B. Add solution B dropwise to solution A, and continue stirring for 30 min. It was repeatedly washed with distilled water and dried to give a red Cu2O precipitate.

nodes.name: PC-0.05 synthesis
nodes.procedure: Solution C was prepared by dissolving 0.05g of copper acetate in 25 mL of distilled water, and stirring at 70°C for 10 min to completely dissolve it. Add 0.5g of P25 to the copper acetate solution and sonicate for 10 min, continue stirring and disperse evenly. In a separate vessel, solution D was prepared by completely dissolving 0.16g NaOH and 0.14g ascorbic acid in 20 mL distilled water, and solution D was added dropwise to the solution C solution, stirring continuously for 30 minutes. Fully washed with distilled water, separated by suction filtration, and collected after drying to obtain sample PC-0.05.

As shown in Fig.6 (a-b), all samples exhibited photocatalytic hydrogen production activity, and the performance of the Cu2O-loaded photocatalyst was significantly better than that of pristine P25. The optimally performing photocatalyst sample PC-0.1 exhibited a hydrogen production of 74.6 mmol·g⁻¹, which is 72 times that of the commercial P25.
The optimally performing photocatalyst sample PC-0.1 exhibited a hydrogen production of 74.6 mmol·g⁻¹, which is 72 times that of the commercial P25.

The photocatalytic stability of sample PC-0.1 was verified by cycling hydrogen production tests, and the results are shown in Fig.6d. Compared with the first cycle value, there was no significant decrease in H2 production after 15h of cycling. It indicates that the sample PC-0.1 has good photocatalytic stability. The XRD spectra of the sample PC-0.1 were measured before and after the cyclic hydrogen production test (Fig.6e). The crystal structure did not change.

nodes.characterization_summary: P25 and PC-0.1 show diffraction peaks of anatase and rutile TiO2; pure Cu2O matches standard card; PC-0.1 lattice constants a=b=3.78733 Å, c=9.49434 Å with no crystal structure change.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig.1b shows the XRD spectra of P25 and the deposited samples with different amounts of Cu2O. Obviously observed diffraction peaks were attributed to anatase and rutile TiO2.

nodes.characterization_summary: PC-0.1 exhibits characteristic Cu2O peak at 1375 cm⁻¹ confirming successful anchoring to P25 surface.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig.1d clearly shows that the sample exhibits a characteristic peak of Cu2O at 1375 cm⁻¹, further indicating that the Cu2O are successfully anchored to the commercial P25 surface.

nodes.characterization_summary: PC-0.1 shows TiO2 Raman peaks at 144, 196, 396, 517, 638 cm⁻¹ with shift to higher wavenumber indicating stronger Cu2O-TiO2 interaction and charge transfer; no Cu oxide peaks detected.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Raman peaks at 144, 196, 396, 517 and 638 cm⁻¹ in Fig.1e were attributed to Eg (1), Eg (2), B1g (1), A1g + B1g (1) and Eg (3).

nodes.characterization_summary: PC-0.1 survey XPS detects Ti, O, C, Cu; Ti 2p peaks at 464 eV (Ti⁴⁺ 2p1/2) and 458 eV (Ti⁴⁺ 2p3/2); Cu 2p shows partial Cu¹⁺→Cu²⁺ oxidation with surface CuO; Cu LMM confirms Cu²⁺ at 566, 570 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig.2a shows that four elements (Ti, O, C and Cu) were detected in sample PC-0.1... Cu¹⁺ at both 566 and 570 eV in Fig.2f, which confirms the stable presence of Cu₂O.

nodes.characterization_summary: PC-0.1 shows uniformly dispersed spherical Cu2O QDs on P25 surface; lattice fringes 0.32 nm (TiO2 110), 0.17 nm (Cu2O 211); average particle size 1.84 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig.3f show that the average particle size of Cu2O is 1.84 nm. Which indicates that the obtained Cu2O is Cu2O QDs.

nodes.characterization_summary: PC-0.1 shows enhanced light absorption in 385-515 nm range compared to P25 (absorption edge ~320 nm).
nodes.evidence_snippet: After the introduction of Cu2O QDs, sample PC-0.1 showed the strongest light absorption in the UV region. The light absorption range was significantly enhanced in the 385-515 nm interval.

nodes.characterization_summary: P25 band gap 3.20 eV; PC-0.1 band gap reduced to 3.03 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The results in Fig.7b show that the energy band gap of P25 is 3.20 eV. The introduction of Cu2O QDs reduces the energy band gap of sample PC-0.1 to 3.03 eV.

nodes.characterization_summary: P25 conduction band -0.63 eV; PC-0.1 conduction band -0.99 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig.7c, the conduction band position of commercial P25 was calculated to be -0.63 eV. The conduction band position of sample PC-0.1 was -0.99 eV.

nodes.characterization_summary: PC-0.1 shows enhanced EPR resonance signal compared to weak P25 signal, indicating more unpaired electrons.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The pure-phase P25 resonance signal is weak, while the identifiable resonance signal is enhanced after deposition of Cu2O QDs.

nodes.characterization_summary: PC-0.1 shows smaller Nyquist arc radius than P25, indicating lower interface resistance and higher charge separation efficiency.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The arc radius of the PC-0.1 sample is smaller than that of P25, indicating that the interface resistance becomes smaller after the deposition of Cu2O QDs.

nodes.characterization_summary: PC-0.1 PL peak diminished and shifted to 513 nm from P25 peak at 475 nm, indicating reduced carrier recombination.
nodes.evidence_snippet: After deposition of Cu2O QDs, the PL peak of the sample gradually diminished. The fluorescence emission peak of sample PC-0.1 shifted to a larger wavelength of 513 nm.

nodes.characterization_summary: P25 specific surface area and pore size distribution unchanged after Cu2O QDs deposition.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The results of nitrogen adsorption and desorption in Fig.S9 and specific surface area in Table S2 show that the specific surface area and pore size distribution of P25 do not change significantly.

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS confirms successful Cu₂O synthesis in PC-0.1 (Fig.S8, Table S1).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The EDS data in Fig.S8 and Table S1 further demonstrate the successful synthesis of Cu₂O.
